title: Start here: basics
subtitle: Variables, types, and operators — the building blocks of Python

concepts.title: What is a variable?
lines: A variable is a name that stores a value.
Now price stands for the number 7:

concepts.title: Name a variable
lines: Names may use letters, digits and _:
A name cannot start with a digit and cannot contain spaces — 2price and my price are errors.

concepts.title: Names are case-sensitive
lines: >>> print(name)          # ERROR: there is no name variable
name and Name are two different variables.

concepts.title: Variables can change
lines: Assign again to update the value:
The new value replaces the old one.

concepts.title: f-strings put values into text
lines: Put f before the quotes and use {} for a value:

exercises.question: Which of these is a valid variable name?
exercises.hint: Spaces, a leading digit and the dash are not allowed.
exercises.explanation: my_age uses only letters and an underscore, and it does not start with a digit.

exercises.hint: print shows the value that x stands for.
exercises.explanation: x was assigned 12, so print(x) shows 12.

exercises.hint: The second assignment replaces the first one.
exercises.explanation: greeting was reassigned to "hello", which overwrites the earlier "hi".

exercises.hint: count + 1 uses the current value of count.
exercises.explanation: count is 5, so count = 5 + 1 makes count equal to 6.

exercises.hint: Subtract the value stored in x from the value stored in y.
exercises.explanation: y is 20 and x is 10, so 20 - 10 is 10.

exercises.prompt: Create a variable name with the value "Ada", then print Hello Ada. using an f-string.
exercises.hint: print(f"Hello {name}.")
exercises.explanation: The f-string slots the value of name into the message: print(f"Hello {name}.").

concepts.title: Every value has a type
lines: Python keeps track of what kind of value you have.
3.14     — a float (number with a decimal point)

concepts.title: Quotes make text
lines: 7 is a number, but "7" is text — same look, different type.

concepts.title: Booleans are capitalised
lines: True and False are written with capital letters.
true or TRUE would both be errors.

exercises.question: What type is the value 1.0?
exercises.hint: It is written with a decimal point.
exercises.explanation: A number written with a decimal point is a float.

exercises.question: What type is the value "42"?
exercises.hint: The quotes turn the value into text.
exercises.explanation: "42" is written inside quotes, so it is a str even though it looks like a number.

exercises.hint: 5 is a whole number.
exercises.explanation: 5 is a whole number, so type(5) reports <class 'int'>.

exercises.hint: True is one of the two boolean values.
exercises.explanation: True is a boolean, so type(True) reports <class 'bool'>.

exercises.hint: int("3") turns the text "3" into the number 3.
exercises.explanation: int("3") converts the text to the number 3, and 3 + 4 is 7.

exercises.hint: float() adds a decimal point to a whole number.
exercises.explanation: float(2) turns the int 2 into the float 2.0.

exercises.prompt: Print the type of the number 3.14. You should see <class 'float'>.
exercises.hint: print(type(3.14))
exercises.explanation: print(type(3.14)) runs type on the value and prints <class 'float'>.

concepts.title: Comparison
lines: Comparison gives back a bool: True or False.

concepts.title: Logical and, or, not
lines: not flips a True to False and a False to True.

concepts.title: Order of operations
lines: Python follows the usual maths order:

exercises.question: What is 7 // 2?
exercises.hint: // divides and rounds down.
exercises.explanation: 7 // 2 is floor division, which gives 3 (it rounds 3.5 down).

exercises.question: What is 7 % 2?
exercises.hint: % gives the remainder after dividing.
exercises.explanation: 7 divided by 2 fits 3 times with 1 left over, so 7 % 2 is 1.

exercises.hint: ** means to the power of.
exercises.explanation: 2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.

exercises.hint: Both comparisons must be True for and to be True.
exercises.explanation: 10 > 5 is True and 3 < 4 is True, so True and True is True.

exercises.hint: Check 1 == 2 first, then apply not.
exercises.explanation: 1 == 2 is False, and not False is True.

exercises.hint: Strings do not add like numbers — + joins text.
exercises.explanation: "3" and "4" are text, so + joins them into the text "34".

exercises.prompt: Print 7 divided by 2 using true division. You should see 3.5.
exercises.hint: print(7 / 2)
exercises.explanation: / is true division, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. (It is // that would give 3.)
